Bibliography

Every source cited on this site, in MLA style, with the lessons that use it. Each lesson lists its own sources at its end under Works Cited.

“’50s progression.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%2750s_progression. Used in: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone, Lesson: Four-Chord Loops (for students)

Ableton. Tuning: An Introduction to Pitch and Tuning Systems. tuning.ableton.com/. Glossary gives the 4:3 fourth vs. 500-cent fourth used in the harmonics-method lesson. Used in: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves, Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament (for students)

“Add Automation Points.” Logic Pro User Guide for Mac, Apple, support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/add-automation-points-lgcpb1a3327b/mac. Used in: DAW 5: The Mixer, DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

“Add, Remove, Move, and Copy Plug-ins.” Logic Pro User Guide for Mac, Apple, support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/add-remove-move-and-copy-plug-ins-lgcpbc218a22/mac. Used in: DAW 5: The Mixer, DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

Adler, Samuel. The Study of Orchestration. 4th ed., W. W. Norton, 2016. Instrument ranges, clefs and transpositions. Used in: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs, Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key, Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs, Score Reading 5: Strange Names (BB♭ Tuba and Friends), Score Reading 6: Practice, Score Reading 3: Transposing Instruments, Part Reader (for teachers)

Aebersold, Jamey. Scale Syllabus. Jamey Aebersold Jazz, www.jazzbooks.com/mm5/download/FREE-scale-syllabus.pdf. Used in: Scale Patterns, Scales

“Akai MPC.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akai_MPC. Used in: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops, Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing, Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch

“Alberti Bass.” Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberti_bass. A broken chord played lowest, highest, middle, highest. Used in: Chord Analysis, Step by Step

“Alberti bass.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberti_bass. Lowest, highest, middle, highest; Classical era; Mozart K. 545. Used in: Style on One Page, Elements 9: Style and Genre, Texture on One Page, Elements 10: Texture (for students)

Aldwell, Edward, Carl Schachter, and Allen Cadwallader. Harmony and Voice Leading. Chapter 27, the source of the examples on the Aldwell and Schachter page. The dataset names the three authors but not the edition, which has not been checked. Used in: Aldwell and Schachter: Harmony and Voice Leading, Analysed Scores (for students)

Aldwell, Edward, Carl Schachter, and Allen Cadwallader. Harmony and Voice Leading. 5th ed., Cengage, 2019. Used in: Lesson: Borrowed Chords, Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not, Lesson: Guide Tones, Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion, Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key, Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody, Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes, Lesson: Write an Ending (for teachers)

Allen, Jont B. “On the Aging of Steel Guitar Strings.” Post to the AUDITORY mailing list, 2005, auditory.org/mhonarc/2005/msg00041.html. Describes Allen’s 1976 Catgut Acoustical Society Newsletter article (not retrieved) and cites J. C. Brown, JASA 95, 1994, p. 2889 (not read). Used in: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

Allingham, Emma, and Clemens Wöllner. “Slow Practice and Tempo-Management Strategies in Instrumental Music Learning: Investigating Prevalence and Cognitive Functions.” Psychology of Music, 2022, doi:10.1177/03057356211073481. doi.org/10.1177/03057356211073481. Abstract and the university’s summary read. Used in: Chunk Practice (for teachers)

Allingham, Emma. Slow Practice in Instrumental Music Learning. 2022. Universität Hamburg, PhD dissertation, ediss.sub.uni-hamburg.de/handle/ediss/9763. Summary read; title as listed there may differ slightly. Used in: Chunk Practice (for teachers)

“Alternate picking.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternate_picking. Used in: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid (for students)

“Alto Saxophone.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone. Used in: Composing 4: Instruments, Ranges and Transposing (for students)

“Amen Break.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amen_break. Used in: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is

Anglebert, Jean-Henry d’. Pièces de clavecin … Livre premier. Paris, 1689. IMSLP. imslp.org/wiki/Pi%C3%A8ces_de_clavecin_(Anglebert,_Jean-Henri_d%27). “Marques des Agrements et leur signification”, read from the 1689 print (IMSLP #110970). Used in: Ornaments by Period (for teachers)

“Annotated Bibliographies.” Purdue Online Writing Lab, Purdue University, owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/common_writing_assignments/annotated_bibliographies/index.html. “Apple Loops in Logic Pro.” Logic Pro User Guide for Mac, Apple, support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/apple-loops-in-logic-pro-lgcp734a05f6/mac. Used in: DAW 7: Bounce, Export and Taking It Further, DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

“Audio Clips, Tempo, and Warping.” Ableton Reference Manual Version 12, Ableton, www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/audio-clips-tempo-and-warping/. Used in: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch

“Audio feedback.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_feedback. Used in: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers, Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA, Live Sound 6: Monitors and Feedback (for students)

“Audio Time Stretching and Pitch Scaling.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_time_stretching_and_pitch_scaling. Used in: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing, Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch

“Augmentation (Music).” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augmentation_(music). Used in: Composing 2: Developing a Motif (for students)

“Automation and Editing Envelopes.” Ableton Reference Manual Version 12, Ableton, www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/automation-and-editing-envelopes/. Used in: DAW 5: The Mixer, DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

“Auto-Tune.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto-Tune. Used in: Sound 21: Pitch Effects (for students)

Azzara, Christopher D., and Richard F. Grunow. Developing Musicianship through Improvisation, Book 1: C Instruments. GIA Publications, 2006. Unit repertoire songs (melody and chords) transcribed into the dmti set of apps/tunes/tunes-object.js: “Mary Ann” (p. 17), “Joshua” (p. 33), “Down by the Riverside” (p. 69); “Long, Long Ago” (p. 1) and “Simple Gifts” (p. 51) were already in the collection. Part 2, Echo Tonal Patterns of Units 4 and 5 (solfège, p. xi), copied into dmti1-unit4-tonal / -unit5-tonal in apps/patterns/pattern-set.js with C as DO (Units 1–3 are the site’s major-I-V and minor-i-V); Echo Rhythm Patterns of Units 1–5 (pp. 2, 18, 34, 52, 71; syllables, pp. vii–ix), dmti1-unit1-rhythm … -unit5-rhythm in apps/rhythms/rhythm-pattern-object.js. MLT Books: the unit, part and Seven Skills structure and the instructions of every unit (pp. v–vi, 1–89), the tunes “Long, Long Ago” (p. 1) and “Simple Gifts” (pp. 51–52) as DMTI prints them (dmti-long-long-ago, dmti-simple-gifts); the examples on the page are generated, not copied. Reproduced with permission. Used in: DMTI: Developing Musicianship through Improvisation, Tune Assessment, Tonal Patterns, Rhythm Sequences, Rhythm Patterns, Tunes

Azzara, Christopher D., and Richard F. Grunow. Developing Musicianship through Improvisation, Book 2: C Instruments. GIA Publications, 2010. Unit repertoire songs (melody and chords) transcribed into the dmti set of apps/tunes/tunes-object.js: “When the Saints Go Marching In” (p. 1) and “Motherless Child” (p. 39); “Amazing Grace” was already in the collection. Part 2, Echo Tonal Patterns of Units 1–3 (solfège, p. ix; the lower of the two octaves printed), dmti2-unit1-tonal … -unit3-tonal in apps/patterns/pattern-set.js with C as DO (C as LA in Unit 3); Echo Rhythm Patterns of Units 1–3 (pp. 2, 22, 40; syllables, pp. vii–viii), dmti2-unit1-rhythm … -unit3-rhythm in apps/rhythms/rhythm-pattern-object.js. MLT Books: “Amazing Grace” as DMTI prints it (p. 21, dmti-amazing-grace, the tune without the upper harmony). Reproduced with permission. Used in: DMTI: Developing Musicianship through Improvisation, Tune Assessment, Tonal Patterns, Rhythm Sequences, Rhythm Patterns, Tunes

Azzara, Christopher D., and Richard F. Grunow. Developing Musicianship through Improvisation, Book 3: C Instruments. GIA Publications, 2010. Unit 1, “Saint Louis Blues”: the twelve Blue Note Patterns (pp. ix, 6), copied into the dmti-blue-notes set of apps/patterns/pattern-set.js with C as DO; the twelve Echo Tonal Patterns of the same page (p. 6, solfège p. ix) are dmti3-unit1-tonal, those of Unit 2 “Transformation” (p. x) dmti3-unit2-tonal and of Unit 3 “Red Wings” (p. xi) dmti3-unit3-tonal (lower octave where two are printed); the Echo Rhythm Patterns of the three units (syllables, pp. vii–viii) are dmti3-unit1-rhythm … -unit3-rhythm in apps/rhythms/rhythm-pattern-object.js. Unit repertoire tunes (melody and chords) transcribed into the dmti set of apps/tunes/tunes-object.js: “Transformation” (p. 23) and “Red Wings” (pp. 47–48), both by Azzara. MLT Books: “Saint Louis Blues” section A (p. 1, dmti-saint-louis-blues, the upper voice an octave down). Reproduced with permission. Used in: DMTI: Developing Musicianship through Improvisation, Tune Assessment, Tonal Patterns, Rhythm Sequences, Rhythm Patterns, Tunes

Bach, Carl Philipp Emanuel. Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments. Translated and edited by William J. Mitchell, W. W. Norton, 1949. First published as Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen, 1753. Ch. 2, Embellishments. Used in: Ornaments by Period (for teachers)

Bach, Johann Sebastian. Clavier-Büchlein vor Wilhelm Friedemann Bach. Manuscript, begun 22 Jan. 1720. Yale University, Irving S. Gilmore Music Library. collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/10991080. The Explication unterschiedlicher Zeichen is on leaf 3v (IIIF image 10991088); the table on this page is read from it. Used in: Ornaments by Period (for teachers)

“Backbeat.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backbeat. Used in: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle, First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone (for students)

“Backdoor progression.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backdoor_progression. Used in: Lesson: Borrowed Chords, Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not (for students)

Bad Mister. “Arpeggiator Key Modes.” Yamaha Synth, Yamaha Corporation of America. yamahasynth.com/learn/moxf-series-music-production-synthesizers/arpeggiator-key-modes-moxf/. Written for the MOXF; the source for what Sort, Thru, Direct, Sort+Direct and Thru+Direct sound, and velocity limits splitting one arp across parts. Used in: Sequencers & Arpeggiators

“Balanced audio.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balanced_audio. Used in: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors (for students)

Barbour, J. Murray. Tuning and Temperament: A Historical Survey. Michigan State College Press, 1951. Used in: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves, Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament (for teachers)

Barry, Nancy H. “The Effects of Practice Strategies, Individual Differences in Cognitive Style, and Gender upon Technical Accuracy and Musicality of Student Instrumental Performance.” Psychology of Music, vol. 20, no. 2, 1992, pp. 112–23. journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0305735692202002. Gordon, Edwin E. Learning Sequences in Music: A Contemporary Music Learning Theory. 2012 ed., GIA Publications, 2012. Skill learning sequence: partial synthesis (pp. 111–117), the verbal association warning (p. 108), generalization-aural/oral and -verbal (pp. 131–133); same is easier to hear than different (p. 219); tonal and rhythm patterns kept apart (p. 223); rhythm patterns chanted with vocal inflection like speech (p. 101); macrobeats stressed, not accented, and approached with a decrescendo, expression found between macrobeats, anacruses given special attention, weight and flow, displaced energy in rests and long durations (pp. 187–190).; Theory Concepts pages: Keyality versus key signature (p. xiii); tonality “best refers to what is usually called a mode,” the eight tonalities (p. 149); movable-do with la-based minor and the rhythm syllables du de, du da di (p. 105); resting tone and tonic, a tonality in any keyality (p. 150); unitonal and multitonal music (pp. 152, 157); usual duple, triple and combined meter (pp. 175–176); no direct relation between measure signatures and meter, 6/8 as “duple compound” called inaccurate (p. 176); accents and microbeat divisions do not make meter (pp. 176–177); unusual meter, paired and unpaired, intact, macrobeats versus microbeats establishing meter (pp. 179–180); key signatures as do signatures, one signature for many tonalities (pp. 155–156); rhythm syllables by beat function (p. 86); time-value names lead to counting (p. 38); writing tonal patterns from a familiar do signature (p. 125); letter names and time-value names as the alphabet of music (pp. 36–37); interval names learned in context of tonality and keyality (p. 65); the raised seventh of harmonic minor as si (p. 70); mi si ti re as a harmonic minor dominant pattern (p. 100).; Course pages (glossary, enrichment): audiation defined and compared with imitation (Introduction; pp. 3, 9); notation as a window (p. 8); patterns as units of meaning (pp. 99–100); the aural/oral level and the pause (pp. 101–102); discrimination and inference learning, theory delayed (p. 106); levels of the skill learning sequence (from pp. 111, 117, 126, 129, 136, 141); stepwise and bridging movement, Table 17 (pp. 230–231).; Hearing Harmony: four stages of readiness for chord changes (p. 305); harmonic patterns I V7 I, I IV I, I II V7 I, I II7 V7 I (p. 313); I V7 I, then I IV I, then I IV V7 I and I V7 IV I in three sung parts, then harmonic minor (pp. 318–319); easy and moderately difficult harmonic patterns, the supertonic delayed (p. 320).; Bass Lines by Ear: macrobeats in usual duple and triple meter (pp. 175–176); same is easier to hear than different (p. 219).
